displayQuote: Love consists of this: two solitudes that meet, protect, and greet each other

meta.title: Who really said "Love consists of this: two solitudes that meet, protect, and greet each other"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Rilke really wrote it — Letter Seven, Rome, 14 May 1904. But his verb was grenzen, to border. The popular "meet" quietly deletes his whole point.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Love consists of this: two solitudes that meet, protect, and greet each other'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Rilke, mangled English. The German says two solitudes protect, border and greet each other — "meet" is a later softening.

answer.label: Rilke wrote it — but not in these words
answer.authorDates: 1875–1926 · Austrian poet, writing from Rome on 14 May 1904
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is genuinely Rilke’s: it closes the argument of Letter Seven to Franz Xaver Kappus, and the German reads der Liebe, die darin besteht, daß zwei Einsamkeiten einander schützen, grenzen und grüßen. But his three verbs are schützen, grenzen, grüßen — protect, border, greet — and the popular English swaps “meet” for “border,” quietly deleting the one verb his whole argument turns on.
answer.confidenceText: Real Rilke, real letter, real date — mangled English.

source.heading: The letter it comes from

docMeta.dd: Briefe an einen jungen Dichter (Letters to a Young Poet)
Letter Seven, to Franz Xaver Kappus — Rome, 14 May 1904
1929, Insel-Verlag, Leipzig — posthumously, gathered by Kappus
M. D. Herter Norton, W. W. Norton, New York, 1934

source.excerpt: Und diese menschlichere Liebe (die unendlich rücksichtsvoll und leise, und gut und klar in Binden und Lösen sich vollziehen wird) wird jener ähneln, die wir ringend und mühsam vorbereiten, der Liebe, die darin besteht, daß zwei Einsamkeiten einander schützen, grenzen und grüßen.
trail: The German primary text is online in full: the letter of 14 May 1904 to Franz Xaver Kappus ↗ closes its argument on love with the sentence der Liebe, die darin besteht, daß zwei Einsamkeiten einander schützen, grenzen und grüßen.
The book was assembled by its recipient and printed after Rilke’s death: first published in 1929 by Insel Verlag in Leipzig ↗, collecting ten letters to Kappus (1883–1966).
The English descends from a named, datable translation: the 1934 W. W. Norton edition ↗, translated by M. D. Herter Norton, catalogued as a translation of Briefe an einen jungen Dichter.
Wikiquote’s sourced Rilke page ↗ dates the surrounding passages — on love as a burden and apprenticeship, and on the coming “female human being” — to the same Letter Seven of 14 May 1904.
source.excerptNote: The three verbs are schützen (protect), grenzen (to border, to form a limit with) and grüßen (to greet or salute). M. D. Herter Norton’s English renders the last clause “protect and border and salute each other,” as printed in a scan of that translation ↗. No translation we checked uses “meet.”

Credit it as shown above; don’t present it as public domain, and get permission for commercial or published reuse.
source.rightsNote: Two different clocks run here. Rilke’s German original was first published in 1929, before the 1931 US cutoff, so the German sentence is public domain in the United States. The standard English, M. D. Herter Norton’s translation, was published by W. W. Norton in 1934 and remains in copyright. The wording asked about matches neither exactly — it is an unattributed English variant of unknown origin — so we assert no rights status for it.

author.name: Rainer Maria Rilke
author.heading: About Rainer Maria Rilke
author.metaLine: 1875–1926 · Austrian poet · wrote in German and French
author.bio: Rilke was born in Prague in 1875 and died near Montreux, Switzerland, in 1926. He is generally reckoned the greatest German-language poet of the early twentieth century, on the strength of The Book of Hours, New Poems, The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge, and the late Duino Elegies and Sonnets to Orpheus. His most-quoted prose, though, is not a book he published: it is a run of ten letters written between 1903 and 1908 to a young officer cadet, printed only after his death.

copyAttribution: Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet, Letter Seven (Rome, 14 May 1904). Rilke's German is "der Liebe, die darin besteht, daß zwei Einsamkeiten einander schützen, grenzen und grüßen" — two solitudes that protect, border and greet each other. The popular "two solitudes that meet" replaces the bordering verb and is not a wording found in the translation we verified. Checked at quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What actually went wrong
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake quote. The author is right, the book is right, the date is right. What has drifted is the English — and it drifted in exactly the place where the sentence carries its meaning.

items.why: Rilke’s German is daß zwei Einsamkeiten einander schützen, grenzen und grüßen, as printed in the letter of 14 May 1904 ↗. Grenzen is to bound, to form a border with. Two solitudes that meet is a different and much softer idea than two solitudes that hold a line between them.

The English sentence that this variant loosens comes from a published translation. The 1934 Norton edition ↗ was translated by M. D. Herter Norton and issued by W. W. Norton in New York; in a readable scan of that translation ↗ the closing clause is “protect and border and salute each other.” Quote cards almost never name a translator at all.

The line normally travels with nothing but Rilke’s name. Yet the letter is precisely locatable: Wikiquote sources a whole run of neighbouring passages ↗ to Letter Seven, 14 May 1904 — the same letter this sentence comes from.

misattribution.truthLine: Rilke did write it, in German, in Letter Seven to Franz Xaver Kappus, Rome, 14 May 1904 ↗ — and he wrote three verbs, not two. Protect, border, greet.

context.heading: Why the missing verb matters
lead: In late 1902 a nineteen-year-old officer cadet at the Theresian Military Academy in Wiener Neustadt, Franz Xaver Kappus (1883–1966) ↗, wrote to Rilke asking whether his poems were any good. Rilke answered him ten times over the next several years, and mostly declined to talk about the poems at all. He talked instead about solitude, patience, and how badly people love.

Letter Seven, written from Rome on 14 May 1904, is the love letter of the sequence — and its argument is that love is not a merging. Young lovers, Rilke says, throw themselves together before either of them is anybody yet. What he wants instead arrives in the letter’s final movement, in a formula built out of three verbs: schützen, grenzen, grüßen. Two solitudes that guard each other, set a limit to each other, and salute each other across it.
context.detailsSummary: How a private letter became the most-quoted thing Rilke wrote
detailsBody: Rilke never prepared these letters for publication. Kappus kept them, and after Rilke’s death in 1926 he gathered and published the ten of them as Briefe an einen jungen Dichter — issued by Insel-Verlag in Leipzig in 1929, according to the publication history of the book ↗.

The first English version came from M. D. Herter Norton, published by W. W. Norton in New York in 1934; the catalogue record for that edition ↗ describes it as a translation of Briefe an einen jungen Dichter, containing letters written to F. X. Kappus during 1903–1908. Nearly every English quotation of the two-solitudes line descends from a translation, and nearly none of them names one.
context.pull: Schützen, grenzen, grüßen. The middle verb is the one the internet drops.

sourcesVerified.claim: Rilke's letter to Franz Xaver Kappus, Rome, 14 May 1904, contains the German sentence 'der Liebe, die darin besteht, daß zwei Einsamkeiten einander schützen, grenzen und grüßen'.

An English edition of Letters to a Young Poet was published by W. W. Norton, New York, in 1934, translated by M. D. Herter Norton, and is catalogued as a translation of Briefe an einen jungen Dichter containing letters written to F. X. Kappus. (The catalogue record is a microfilm entry: it supports translator, publisher and year, but carries no readable text and no 'first edition' statement.)

A scan of the M. D. Herter Norton translation (copyright 1934, W. W. Norton; revised edition 1954) renders the closing clause of Letter Seven, dated Rome, May 14th, 1904, as 'the love that consists in this, that two solitudes protect and border and salute each other'.

Letters to a Young Poet was first published in 1929 by Insel Verlag in Leipzig; the recipient was Franz Xaver Kappus (1883–1966), a nineteen-year-old officer cadet at the Theresian Military Academy in Wiener Neustadt.
Wikiquote's Rilke page sources a run of passages on love and on the 'feminine human being' to Letter Seven (14 May 1904); it does not carry the 'two solitudes' line.

Rainer Maria Rilke was born 4 December 1875 in Prague and died 29 December 1926 near Montreux, Switzerland; he wrote in German and French, and his principal works include The Book of Hours, New Poems, The Notebooks of Malte Laurids Brigge, Duino Elegies and Sonnets to Orpheus.
